plan: Gaps: IES 4, Functions 2, N&Q 1, Algebra 1, Geometry 1, S&P 1. Hard share still low, so 6 hard / 4 medium. Hard: rate per hen-day, chained gear ratios, conditional percent among responders, degenerate quadratic (k ≠ 0), exponential vs linear comparison with an equality boundary, continuous probability on an interval.

candidates.stem: Three hens lay a total of 3 eggs in 3 days. At this same rate per hen, how many eggs will 6 hens lay in 6 days?
candidates.explanation: 3 hens × 3 days = 9 hen-days produce 3 eggs, so each hen-day produces 1/3 egg. Then 6 hens × 6 days = 36 hen-days produce 36 × 1/3 = 12 eggs.

A.rationale: This doubles only once, as if doubling both hens and days doubled the eggs; doubling each one doubles the output, so the total quadruples.

B.rationale: This adds 3 eggs for each doubling instead of multiplying.

D.rationale: 36 is the number of hen-days, not eggs; each hen-day yields only 1/3 egg.

hints: How many eggs does one hen lay in one day?
Multiply that rate by the number of hens and the number of days.
candidates.remember: Double the workers and double the time: four times the output.

author_checklist.hardness: strong intuitive trap (6); requires a per-unit rate

candidates.stem: Gear A has 36 teeth and meshes with gear B, which has 24 teeth. Gear B is fixed to the same axle as gear C, so B and C always turn together at the same rate. Gear C has 30 teeth and meshes with gear D, which has 15 teeth. If gear A turns at 40 revolutions per minute, how many revolutions per minute does gear D turn?
candidates.explanation: Meshing gears pass the same number of teeth per minute. A: 36 × 40 = 1,440 teeth per minute, so B turns 1,440 ÷ 24 = 60 rpm. C shares B's axle, so C also turns at 60 rpm, passing 30 × 60 = 1,800 teeth per minute. D turns 1,800 ÷ 15 = 120 rpm.

A.rationale: This assumes all the gears turn at the same rate as gear A.

B.rationale: 60 rpm is the speed of gears B and C; the last mesh with gear D has not been applied.

C.rationale: This applies only the C-to-D ratio to gear A's speed (40 × 30/15 = 80), skipping the A-to-B mesh.

hints: When two gears mesh, teeth × revolutions per minute is the same for both.
Gears on the same axle turn at the same rate, whatever their sizes.
candidates.remember: Meshed gears: teeth × rpm is equal. Same axle: rpm is equal.

author_checklist.hardness: two different rules (mesh vs shared axle) applied in sequence

candidates.subskill: Tax and tip on the same base
candidates.stem: A restaurant bill is $60.00 before tax. Sales tax is 8% of the $60.00, and the diners also leave a tip equal to 20% of the $60.00. What is the total amount the diners pay?

A.rationale: $72.00 includes the tip but leaves out the tax.

C.rationale: This takes the tip on the after-tax amount (60 × 1.08 × 1.20), but the tip is based on the $60.00.

D.rationale: This adds 48% of $60 by counting the 20% tip twice.

hints: Both percents are of the same $60.00.
Add the tax and the tip to the bill.
candidates.remember: Percents of the same base can be added.

author_checklist.dup_note: the app fixture applies a discount then tax to a jacket price; this item adds two percents on one base

candidates.stem: In a survey, 40% of the respondents were students. Of the students, 25% said they use public transit daily; of the respondents who were not students, 10% said they use public transit daily. Of the respondents who said they use public transit daily, what percent were students?
candidates.explanation: Imagine 1,000 respondents: 400 students and 600 non-students. Daily transit users: 25% of 400 = 100 students and 10% of 600 = 60 non-students, 160 in all. The fraction who are students is 100/160 = 62.5%.

A.rationale: 25% is the percent of students who use transit daily; the question reverses the condition.

B.rationale: 40% is the share of students among all respondents, not among daily transit users.

D.rationale: This compares the two percents directly, 25/(25 + 10), ignoring that there are more non-students.

hints: Pick a convenient total, such as 1,000 respondents, and count people.
Restrict attention to the people who use transit daily.

strategy.explanation: With 1,000 respondents: 100 student users and 60 other users; 100 ÷ 160.

candidates.remember: Reverse a condition by counting actual people.

author_checklist.hardness: reversed conditional with unequal group sizes; three strong traps

candidates.subskill: Scientific notation in a rate conversion
candidates.stem: Light travels about 3.0 × 10⁵ kilometers per second. About how many kilometers does light travel in 1 hour?

A.rationale: This divides by 60 instead of multiplying.

B.rationale: 1.8 × 10⁷ is the distance in 1 minute; it must still be multiplied by 60.

hints: How many seconds are in an hour?
Multiply the leading numbers and add the exponents, then adjust so the leading number is between 1 and 10.

candidates.stem: For which values of the constant k does the equation kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 have exactly two distinct real solutions?
candidates.explanation: If k = 0, the equation is 4x + 1 = 0, which has only one solution. If k ≠ 0, the equation is quadratic and has two distinct real solutions when the discriminant is positive: 16 − 4k > 0, so k < 4. Together: k < 4 and k ≠ 0.

B.rationale: This misses that k = 0 makes the equation linear, with just one solution.

C.rationale: This reverses the discriminant inequality; k > 4 gives no real solutions.

D.rationale: k = 4 makes the discriminant 0, giving one repeated solution, not two distinct ones; k = 0 is also wrong.

hints: When does a quadratic have two distinct real solutions?
What kind of equation is it when k = 0?

strategy.explanation: Test k = 0 (one solution: rules out B and D) and k = 5 (no real solutions: rules out C).

candidates.remember: A quadratic's leading coefficient cannot be 0.

author_checklist.hardness: degenerate-case insight beyond the routine discriminant

candidates.stem: Let f(x) = 2^x and g(x) = 4x. For how many integers x with 1 ≤ x ≤ 10 is f(x) ≥ g(x) ?
candidates.explanation: Compare values: x = 1: 2 < 4; x = 2: 4 < 8; x = 3: 8 < 12; x = 4: 16 = 16; x = 5: 32 > 20; and 2^x keeps growing faster after that. So f(x) ≥ g(x) for x = 4, 5, …, 10: that is 7 integers.

A.rationale: 3 counts the integers where f(x) < g(x), the opposite condition.

B.rationale: This leaves out x = 4, where the two values are equal; the condition includes equality.

D.rationale: This assumes the exponential is always at least as large, but for x = 1, 2 and 3 it is smaller.

hints: Make a small table of 2^x and 4x for x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Watch for the value of x where they are equal.

strategy.explanation: Table: (2, 4), (4, 8), (8, 12), (16, 16), (32, 20): the exponential catches up at 4 and stays ahead.

candidates.remember: Exponentials start slow, then overtake linear functions.

author_checklist.hardness: crossover with an equality case; both 'opposite' and 'strict' traps

candidates.stem: A function f is called odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for every real number x. Which of the following functions is odd?
candidates.explanation: For f(x) = x³ − x: f(−x) = (−x)³ − (−x) = −x³ + x = −(x³ − x) = −f(x), so it is odd. The others fail: x² + 1 and |x| satisfy f(−x) = f(x) (even), and for x³ + 1, f(−1) = 0 but −f(1) = −2.

A.rationale: x² + 1 is even: f(−x) = f(x), not −f(x).

C.rationale: x³ is odd, but adding 1 breaks the property: f(−1) = 0 while −f(1) = −2.

hints: Replace x with −x in each function and simplify.
Is the result the negative of the original function?

strategy.explanation: Test x = 2 and x = −2: x³ − x gives 6 and −6 (opposites); x³ + 1 gives 9 and −7; the even functions give equal outputs.

candidates.remember: Odd functions: f(−x) = −f(x); their graphs are symmetric about the origin.

candidates.stem: A closed rectangular box has inside dimensions 3 inches by 4 inches by 12 inches. What is the length, in inches, of the longest straight rod that fits completely inside the box?
candidates.explanation: The longest rod lies along the box's space diagonal: √(3² + 4² + 12²) = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = 13 inches.

A.rationale: 5 is the diagonal of the 3-by-4 face, not the whole box.

B.rationale: 12 is the longest edge; the diagonal through the box is longer.

D.rationale: 19 adds the three dimensions; a straight line is shorter than a path along the edges.

hints: The longest segment goes from one corner to the opposite corner.
Use the Pythagorean theorem twice, or the three-dimensional version.

author_checklist.dup_note: the bank's cube item (CLD-ACT-M-000074) goes from diagonal to volume; this is a non-cube box in context

candidates.stem: A real number x is chosen at random from the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 10, with every number equally likely. What is the probability that x² < 30 ?
candidates.explanation: For x ≥ 0, x² < 30 means x < √30 ≈ 5.48. The favorable part of the interval has length √30 out of a total length of 10, so the probability is √30/10 ≈ 0.548.

A.rationale: This divides by 20, as if x could range from −10 to 10; the interval here starts at 0.

B.rationale: This compares 30 with 10² = 100, treating x² as if it were equally likely to be any value from 0 to 100.

C.rationale: 1/2 assumes the cutoff is the midpoint 5, but √30 ≈ 5.48.

hints: Rewrite x² < 30 as a condition on x itself.
Probability = favorable length ÷ total length.
candidates.remember: Uniform on an interval: probability = favorable length ÷ total length.

author_checklist.hardness: translate a quadratic condition to an interval and use length ratio
